content_voiceover: This diagram explains why unfractionated heparin and low molecular weight heparin behave differently despite sharing the same core mechanism. Both contain a pentasaccharide sequence that binds antithrombin and induces a conformational change, dramatically accelerating antithrombin's ability to inhibit clotting factors. Unfractionated heparin is a long chain, so after it binds antithrombin through the pentasaccharide, the remaining length of the molecule can also wrap around and bind thrombin directly, forming a ternary complex that inhibits both factor Xa and thrombin, or factor IIa, roughly equally. Low molecular weight heparin, shown in the bottom panel, is too short to simultaneously bind both antithrombin and thrombin, so it can only potentiate antithrombin's inhibition of factor Xa, not thrombin. This structural difference explains the classic board fact that unfractionated heparin has an anti-Xa to anti-IIa ratio of about one to one, while LMWH has a ratio favoring anti-Xa activity, around three or four to one, which is also why aPTT monitors UFH well but doesn't reliably reflect LMWH activity, and anti-Xa levels are used instead when needed.
keypoints: Both UFH and LMWH bind antithrombin via a pentasaccharide sequence
UFH is long enough to also bind thrombin directly, inhibiting both Xa and IIa equally
LMWH is too short to bind thrombin, so it selectively inhibits factor Xa
UFH anti-Xa:anti-IIa ratio is about 1:1; LMWH favors anti-Xa
keypoint_voiceover: The core distinction: chain length. Unfractionated heparin is long enough to bridge antithrombin and thrombin, inhibiting Xa and IIa equally, while low molecular weight heparin is too short and mainly inhibits factor Xa, which is why LMWH doesn't reliably prolong the aPTT.
